# Lessons in parts (2026-10)

<!-- Generated by tools/cas-ccps/render-parts-drafts.js from
     cas-ccps/curriculum/lessons/PARTS.json and PARTS_DRAFTS.json; edit the JSON, not this file. -->

Every lesson split into parts (35; `meta/STUDENT_WORK_PLAN_2026-10.md`, Phase 3).
Each part is its own assignment and work file; its **primary** unlocks the next part. Every
lesson competency is in some part. The first lesson, 8177 Market Research, is the pattern
(Appendix B, approved 2026-10-27); the other 34 were drafted in it and approved together on
2026-10-28, to be edited as they are taught. Edit a lesson in `PARTS.json`, run
`node tools/cas-ccps/build-lesson-assignments.js`, then this file's generator.

The "Still open" lines are questions the drafts raised, left for when each lesson is taught.

## Across lessons

- **Text after the last part lands in the last part.** The builder gives each part the paragraphs from its "Part n:" to the next one, so a closing paragraph goes to the last part even when it is about an earlier one: 8175's "Submission: … paste into the submission box", 8177 notes such as "Your budget is confidential" (The Bottom Line), "Everything on a resume must be true" (The Final Whistle), "Do not contact any of these businesses" (The Sponsorship Negotiation), and the labeling rules in The NIL Deal and The Franchise Evolution. To do as each lesson is next edited: move each such line into the part it belongs to in the prompt file, and drop 8175's Submission line, which CAS replaces.
- **"Add the link to this document" no longer fits a part whose work file is a Form, Slides or Sheet.** Until Phase 4 makes those the work files, a non-doc part is still a doc with the link pasted in, so the wording can stay for now; it changes with Phase 4.
- **Parts that build on earlier parts.** Many later parts use an earlier part's work (a survey, a budget, a persona, a map). The student keeps every earlier part's doc, and Flow 2 now reads the earlier parts when it checks a later one (#316); some tasks may still want a line telling the student to bring the numbers forward.
- **Live activities and role-plays.** Parts done in class with others (a negotiation, a role-play, an event) can only be checked through what the student writes about them, and a student who was absent can't do them. The teacher's unlock ("Open Part n now" on the Teacher Dashboard) is the way past one; the lessons below name each case.
- **Optional competencies as primaries.** Where the teacher plan marks a competency "(Optional)" but it is the only fit for a part, the draft makes it that part's primary, so the student must meet it to go on (named in the lessons where it happens).

## L01 EVOLUTION OF MARKETING (FROM TRADE TO TIKTOK)

`8175-L01` · approved 2026-10-28 (draft 1 of 2026-10-28; all 34 approved together, to be edited as they are taught)

| Part | Work file | Primary (unlocks the next part) | Secondary | Tertiary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. The Timeline | Doc | 8175-39 Explain marketing as it relates to the sports, entertainment, and event industries | — | 8175-45 Describe the past, present, and future of the sports, entertainment, and event industries |
| 2. The Shift | Doc | 8175-41 Describe the marketing concept as related to the sports, entertainment, and event industries | — | — |
| 3. The Future | Doc | 8175-47 Analyze trends and innovations in the sports, entertainment, and event industries | 8175-11 Demonstrate big-picture thinking | 8175-45 Describe the past, present, and future of the sports, entertainment, and event industries |
| 4. The Functions | Doc | 8175-43 Describe the marketing functions | — | — |

**Why:** Part 1 is the timeline of the seven eras, so explaining marketing as it relates to the industry (39) is its primary, with tying it to the industry's past (45) as an extra. Part 2 is the Selling Era against the Marketing Company Era, the marketing concept (41). Part 3's prediction is built from AI, virtual reality and privacy laws, so analyzing trends (47) is its primary, with big-picture thinking (11) and past-to-future (45) behind it. Part 4 is the seven functions with two examples (43).

**Criteria in a student's words:**

- **Part 1**
  - *(required)* For each of the seven eras, from the Trade Era to the Collaboration Era, you give its time period and its primary focus in one sentence. (8175-39)
  - *(not required)* You show how the eras connect, so a reader can see how marketing moved from trading goods to working with customers. (8175-45)
- **Part 2**
  - *(required)* You explain the difference between the Selling Era and the Marketing Company Era, and say what businesses started doing for customers instead of tricking them into buying. (8175-41)
- **Part 3**
  - *(required)* You name the next era of marketing and back up your prediction with at least one real trend: AI, virtual reality or privacy laws. (8175-47)
  - Your 3 sentences say how that trend could change the way businesses treat the people they market to. (8175-11)
  - *(not required)* You link your prediction to how sports or entertainment marketing has already changed. (8175-45)
- **Part 4**
  - *(required)* You name all seven functions of marketing, pick two, and give a real sports or entertainment example of each. (8175-43)

**Why:** Parts 1 and 3 are the invention itself (1): the event and who it's for, then the board with all its pieces, with the two logo versions for a jersey or sign and a ticket or app as promotion (97). Part 2's three words are how customers should feel, so what motivates them (93) leads there. Part 4 is the brand decisions others can follow (42), with the venue's atmospherics (45) as secondary and the big picture (11) and accurate brand terms (21) as bonuses. **Criteria in a student's words:**

- **Part 1** (terms: brand)
  - *(required)* You invent an original event or venue and describe it in two or three sentences, including who it is for. (8177-1)
  - *(not required)* You say what would make those customers want to come. (8177-93)
- **Part 2** (terms: brand identity)
  - *(required)* You choose three adjectives for how you want customers to feel and explain why you chose each one. (8177-93)
- **Part 3** (terms: color palette, typography, logo)
  - *(required)* Your board has all of it: five colors, one font, two logo versions, your three words and four images of the customer's experience. (8177-1)
  - You label one logo version for a jersey or sign and the other for a digital ticket or app. (8177-97)
- **Part 4** (terms: brand, brand identity, color palette, typography, logo, atmospherics)
  - *(required)* For your colors, your font and your images, you explain how each choice matches your three words. (8177-42)
  - You explain how your colors and logo would show up inside the venue: on walls, in lighting, or on signs and screens. (8177-45)
  - *(not required)* You explain how one consistent look across tickets, signs, jerseys and posts shapes what customers think of the whole event or venue. (8177-11)
  - *(not required)* You use brand, brand identity, color palette, typography, logo and atmospherics accurately in clear, complete sentences. (8177-21)

| Part | Work file | Primary (unlocks the next part) | Secondary | Tertiary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. The Team | Doc | 8177-95 Analyze personnel needs for an event | — | 8177-5 Demonstrate work ethic |
| 2. Open and Close | Doc | 8177-25 Examine aspects of financial responsibility within an industry/organization | 8177-45 Explain facilities management as it relates to the sports, entertainment, and event industries | 8177-72 Explain how the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) has influenced the planning of events and design of facilities; 8177-73 Explain how legal requirements influence operations in the sports, entertainment, and event industries |
| 3. Integrity and Shrink | Doc | 8177-25 Examine aspects of financial responsibility within an industry/organization | 8177-4 Demonstrate integrity | — |
| 4. The Rush | Doc | 8177-58 Demonstrate customer-service techniques | 8177-10 Collaborate with team members; 8177-14 Manage time and resources | 8177-20 Demonstrate professionalism |

**Why:** Part 1 is staffing (95): each role's responsibility and what goes wrong without it. Parts 2 and 3 are financial responsibility (25): the Z-Out, then the Two-Person and scan-everything rules against shrink, with the opening procedures (45) and the laws behind the first step (72, 73) in Part 2 and honesty with cash and stock (4) in Part 3. Part 4 is customer service in the rush (58), with who does what (10) and the order of the plan (14) as secondaries. **Criteria in a student's words:**

- **Part 1** (terms: FIFO, facing)
  - *(required)* For each of the four roles (General Manager, Shift Manager, Sales Associate, Inventory Specialist), you give one responsibility and explain what goes wrong if nobody does it. (8177-95)
  - *(not required)* You show how one person skipping their part, like a restock or leaving the drawer open, causes trouble for the whole team. (8177-5)
- **Part 2** (terms: SOP, float, Z-Out)
  - *(required)* You explain the Z-Out in your own words: what gets counted, that the float is subtracted, and that the result is checked against the daily sales report. (8177-25)
  - You list the four opening procedures in the right order, starting with clearing the 36-inch walkways. (8177-45)
  - *(not required)* You say why the 36-inch walkways have to be completely clear of boxes before the shop opens. (8177-72)
  - *(not required)* You name the ADA and fire code as the rules behind the first opening step. (8177-73)
- **Part 3** (terms: shrink)
  - *(required)* You explain the Two-Person Rule and the scan-everything rule and, for each one, describe a real problem it prevents. (8177-25)
  - You explain how the two rules keep the shop honest with its cash and stock, even for a free giveaway. (8177-4)
- **Part 4**
  - *(required)* You write exactly what you'd say to the customers waiting in line, and it is polite, calm and professional. (8177-58)
  - You say who does what during the rush, so the line and the jammed register are both handled. (8177-10)
  - You put your rush plan in a clear order so the line keeps moving while the register gets fixed. (8177-14)
  - *(not required)* What you say to the customers uses polished language, not slang, like the handbook's greeting. (8177-20)

- 45 (facilities management) is tertiary for the lesson but secondary in Part 2, since half of Part 2 is the four opening procedures in order; confirm or move it to tertiary.

  - *(required)* Your staffing chart lists every role (shift lead, cashier, sales floor/runner, inventory and setup), who fills it and who backs them up. (8177-95)
  - You give a supply list, goals for items sold, revenue, customers and longest wait, and one risk with a backup plan. (8177-100)
- **Part 3** (terms: follow-up, recognition)
  - *(required)* You list everyone who helped and what each did, type a thank-you note to one staff member saying what they did and why it mattered, and draft a public thank-you. (8177-99)

  - *(required)* You compare each goal from Part 2 with the real number from the event log and say whether it was met. (8177-101)

  - You describe what you did during your shift to help the team. (8177-10)
- **Part 5**
  - *(required)* You name one thing to keep and one thing to change for the next event and explain each one using the event's results. (8177-101)

**Still open:**

- The pop-up is a live event between Part 2 and Part 3; Part 3 can't start until it happens, whatever Part 2's result, and an absent student has nothing to write for Parts 3 and 4.
- Parts 1 and 2 (run of show, staffing chart, supply list, goals) are likely planned as a class or team; the teacher should decide whether each student submits their own.
- Part 3's thank-you note is handwritten and delivered; only its typed words can be checked.
- Part 4 compares results with Part 2's goals and the event log; the reader needs both in Part 4's file.

| 4. The Winning Strategy | **Slides** | 8177-94 Explain how event popularity and competitive factors relate to attendance | 8177-2 Demonstrate critical thinking and problem-solving; 8177-93 Describe factors that motivate consumers to attend sports, entertainment, and event occasions | — |

**Why:** Parts 1 and 2 are about what gets the persona off the couch (who they are and what one outing costs them, then their top motivator), so 93 is their primary. Part 3 is the competitor that threatens attendance, so 94 is its primary, with the 'why it's a real threat' as critical thinking (2). Part 4 is the winning promotion against that competitor (94), with fitting it to the budget as problem-solving (2) and matching the motivator (93) as secondaries.

**Criteria in a student's words:**

- **Part 1** (terms: consumer persona, discretionary income)
  - *(required)* You describe your persona: who they are, what a typical week looks like for them, and how much of their monthly budget one outing to your event would cost. (8177-93)
- **Part 2** (terms: motivator, consumer persona)
  - *(required)* You pick one of the five motivators as your persona's top reason to go out and explain, with details from their life, why it fits them. (8177-93)
- **Part 3** (terms: indirect competition, direct competition, discretionary income)
  - *(required)* You name one specific local indirect competitor that could win your persona's money on a Friday night instead of your event. (8177-94)
  - You explain why that competitor is a real threat for this persona: what it offers them that your event doesn't, in time, money or fun. (8177-2)
- **Part 4** (terms: motivator, indirect competition, discretionary income, consumer persona)
  - *(required)* You describe one specific promotion or experience the event could offer and say why it would make your persona choose the event over your competitor. (8177-94)
  - You show the promotion fits your persona's budget: what the outing would cost them with it and how that compares with their monthly budget. (8177-2)
  - You explain how the promotion matches the top motivator you picked for your persona. (8177-93)

- Parts 3 and 4 build on the persona chosen in Part 1 and the motivator in Part 2; a reader of Part 4 alone needs the student to name them again.
